data.caption: Mediator centralizes communication

data.text: Turing a Web of Dependencies into a Hub

Without a mediator, every component that needs to talk to another must know about it, so the number of connections grows faster than the number of components. A mediator puts all those connections in one place: components publish to the mediator and subscribe to what they care about, and they never reference each other.

data.title: A chat room mediator

data.text: Mediator, Observer, and an Event Bus

A mediator is often implemented with observers internally: the mediator is a subject and the components are observers. An event bus is the same idea applied application-wide, except it centralizes on an event name rather than on a domain concept. That distinction matters, because an event bus that everything listens to becomes impossible to reason about.

data.title: The mediator as a small event hub
The mediator can become a god object
data.text: Centralizing communication removes direct coupling but adds coupling to the mediator, which every component now depends on and which grows with every feature. When a single object knows everything and everything knows it, it is hard to test and hard to change. The honest trade-off is that a mediator simplifies a dense graph and becomes a bottleneck when it is asked to do too much.
